title: Akrura Reports to Kamsa
story:
One moment the river had shown Akrura everything, and the next it was gone. The vision he had seen beneath the water — the forms that filled all creation — was withdrawn as suddenly as it had come, folded away the way an actor folds away a play. He rose quickly from the Yamuna, the water streaming from him, and found Krishna standing on the bank as if nothing at all had happened.

"What did you see?" Krishna asked him. "You look as though you have seen something wonderful."

Akrura could barely answer. Everything that can be wondered at, he said, whether on the earth, in the sky, or in the water, stands there in you. He had gone looking for the source of all wonders, and found it standing before him on the bank — not in the river, not beneath the water, but there in the boy who had sent him down into it. The vision had been withdrawn, but the one who contained it had not moved from his side. What had been shown to him in the water remained with him on the land, and he understood now that the river had been only a mirror. He was still turning it over in his mind as he climbed back onto the chariot and, wondering, urged the horses on toward the city. The reins felt strange in his hands; the road ahead felt like the road into a dream.

On the road the village people gathered here and there to see them pass, and the people of Vraja — Nanda and the cowherds — went on ahead. Word of the arrival had run before them, and here and there along the way folk came out to catch sight of the chariot and its passengers, the boys of Vraja on their way to Mathura at last. Then Krishna spoke to Akrura. "You go on," he said. "Enter the city first, with your chariot, and go to your own house."

Akrura would not let it go so easily. Come with us, Lord, he pleaded, and make our homes not without a master, for we are householders and our houses are nothing without you. Purify them with the dust of your feet. Great Bali won lasting fame only by washing those feet, and the water that washed them purified the three worlds. O God of gods, whose very name is auspicious to hear and to sing, do not pass our doors. It was the voice of a man who had just seen the whole of creation gathered in one place and could not bear to see that place ride past his own threshold.

But Krishna sent him on ahead, and Akrura obeyed, though he would rather have stayed. He had asked, and the answer had been given gently and firmly, and there was nothing in his devotion that did not know how to take the answer. The command was gentle, but it was a command, and he had been trusted with an errand. In the afternoon Krishna entered Mathura with Balarama beside him. Akrura, going before them into the city, delivered his account to the king who had sent him — and only then, his errand done, did he turn toward his own house, carrying the wonder he had seen in the river quietly and unspoken within him, the way a man keeps a lamp he has been given to guard.
reflection: Akrura had been shown the whole of creation in the river, and then it was hidden again — revealed and withdrawn, as if it were something that could not yet be spoken of openly. He drove on as he was asked, made his report, and kept the wonder privately inside him.
next_story_tease: But Nanda, having delivered his tribute, would prepare to return to Vraja.
hero_scene: Akrura surfacing from the waters of the Yamuna, dazed, while Krishna watches him with calm amusement; behind them the waiting chariot, and ahead the road and gates of Mathura.
visual_elements: Akrura rising from the water in wonder
Krishna and Balarama on the bank
the road and gates of Mathura
